opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a nice heuristic here that falls out of thinking about the tradeoff economically. You can substitute between training and inference compute to some degree. If you train a bigger model or train it for longer, you get better performance per unit of inference. Alternatively, you can take a smaller model and spend more at inference time, with things like chain-of-thought, sampling many outputs and picking the best one, search, or longer reasoning traces, and recover a lot of that performance.

When you have two inputs that substitute for each other like that, the cost-minimizing allocation usually has you spending roughly comparable amounts on each, at least within an order of magnitude. If you're spending vastly more on one, you're probably at a point where the marginal dollar would buy more capability on the other side. So with some colleagues I've argued that, as a rough rule of thumb, you'd expect labs to spend similar amounts on training and inference overall.

There are some nuances. One is scale of deployment. A training run is a fixed cost amortized over every query you serve. If you're serving hundreds of millions of users, that pushes you toward training a model that's somewhat overtrained relative to the compute-optimal Chinchilla point, because a smaller, cheaper-to-run model saves you a lot over the deployment lifetime. That's part of why we've seen labs train smaller models on far more tokens than the original scaling laws would suggest.

Another is how much the tradeoff varies across tasks. For some tasks, like math, coding, and things with verifiable answers, inference-time compute buys you a lot, and the exchange rate between training and inference is quite favorable. For other tasks, extra thinking doesn't help much and you really need a more capable base model. So the right balance differs by domain.

The bigger-picture point, which matters for thinking about AI's trajectory, is that inference compute isn't just a cost of serving; it's also a lever on capabilities. If you can turn more inference into better performance, the capabilities available at a given time depend not only on the largest training run but on how much compute you're willing to throw at a problem at runtime. That has implications for forecasting, and for governance approaches that focus purely on training compute thresholds, because those may miss a meaningful part of where capability comes from.

r001.rationale: It recommends spending “similar amounts” on training and inference and says they should be roughly comparable, communicating the same-order balance.

r002.rationale: It says that when spending is vastly greater on one side, a marginal dollar would buy more capability on the other, supporting reallocating training-heavy spending to inference for greater capability at the same total cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more interesting questions in thinking about how AI progress is going to unfold over the next few years, and I'd say the honest answer is that there isn't a fixed ratio you should aim for. The right balance is something that shifts over time, and it depends a lot on where you are on various curves.

Let me try to lay out how I think about it. Historically, training compute has been the thing people have focused on, and for good reason. We've seen training compute for frontier models growing at something like four to five times per year, and that scaling has been one of the main drivers of capability gains. So for a long time, the natural thing to do if you wanted a more capable system was to pour more compute into the training run.

But what's become increasingly clear over the past couple of years is that inference compute is a substitute for training compute in a lot of important ways. You can get a model to perform better on a task by having it think longer, sample more candidates, do search, verify its own outputs, and so on. And the exchange rate there is actually quite favorable in some domains. There's work showing that you can match the performance of a model that's an order of magnitude larger just by spending more at inference time on a smaller model, at least for certain kinds of problems. So that opens up a trade-off that didn't really exist as sharply before.

Now, the key economic point is that these two forms of spending have really different cost structures. Training is a fixed cost. You pay it once and then you have the model. Inference is a variable cost that scales with how much you use the system. So the optimal allocation depends enormously on how much deployment you're going to do. If you're going to run a model across hundreds of millions of users, then even small improvements in inference efficiency, or small reductions in how much inference compute you need per task, pay off enormously. In that regime, it makes sense to spend a lot more on training to produce a model that's cheaper to run. That's roughly the logic behind over-training smaller models relative to what the naive scaling laws would suggest.

On the other hand, if what you care about is pushing the frontier of what's possible on hard tasks, where you're not deploying at massive scale but you really need the best answer, then inference scaling looks very attractive, because you're not paying that cost over and over.

I'd also add that at the level of the whole economy, I think we're going to see the share of compute going to inference rise substantially. Right now a very large fraction of frontier compute still goes into training, but as these systems become more useful and get deployed more widely, and especially as you get agents doing long-horizon tasks that consume a lot of tokens, the demand for inference compute is going to grow very quickly. My guess is that within a few years, inference will dominate total compute spending, and that has real implications for hardware, for energy, for where data centers get built.

One more thing I'd flag is that these aren't fully independent anymore. The inference-time techniques that work well, like reinforcement learning on reasoning, actually feed back into training. You use inference compute to generate better data and then train on it. So the line between the two is getting blurry, and I think the right framing is less "how do we split the budget" and more "what's the marginal return on the next dollar in each bucket right now," and being willing to update that as the technology and the deployment picture change.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a fixed ratio and says the balance depends on deployment scale and marginal returns; it never states that inference spending should be roughly half to equal training spending.

r002.rationale: It describes inference compute as a substitute for training compute and gives ways extra inference can improve performance, but does not say that shifting budget from training to inference improves performance at the same total cost.

astra-6.text:
I think the right way to think about this is that training is a fixed cost, whereas inference is a cost you incur each time you use the model. So the balance depends quite a lot on how much use you expect the model to get.

If you're training a model that will serve billions of requests, it can make sense to spend more on training to make each subsequent inference cheaper. You might train a smaller model for longer, for example, rather than train a larger model that's more expensive to run. Even a small saving per request can then justify a substantial additional investment in training.

But inference compute can also improve the quality of an answer. You can give a model more time to work through a problem, generate multiple candidates, or check its work. For a particularly valuable or difficult task, that extra computation might be worth much more than it would be for a simple query.

So I wouldn't expect there to be a single optimal ratio. You want to compare the marginal benefit of spending more on training, which potentially improves every future interaction, with the marginal benefit of spending more at inference time, which you can target toward particular problems. The best allocation depends on the volume of requests, the kinds of tasks, and how much better performance is worth.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no single optimal ratio and gives no estimate that inference spending should be roughly half of or equal to training spending.

r002.rationale: It compares the marginal benefits of training and inference spending, but does not say that shifting budget from training to inference can improve performance at the same total cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right way to think about this is that training is a fixed investment, whereas inference is a cost you incur every time you use the model. So the balance depends a lot on how much use you expect the model to get.

If you’re going to serve billions of requests, it can make sense to spend more on training to produce a smaller, more efficient model. You incur that cost once, and then the savings accumulate across all those requests. If you’re building a model for a relatively narrow application with limited demand, you might prefer to spend less on training and tolerate a higher cost per query.

There’s also a tradeoff in capabilities. You can improve performance by training a better model, but you can also give an existing model more compute at inference time—for example, by letting it consider multiple possible solutions and check its work. The relevant question is which additional dollar delivers more value for the tasks you care about.

So I wouldn’t expect there to be a single optimal ratio. You want to optimize training and inference jointly, taking into account expected demand, the cost of serving the model, and how much additional inference compute actually improves its answers.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no single optimal ratio and gives no claim that inference spending should be roughly half to equal training spending.

r002.rationale: It notes that inference-time compute can improve a model’s performance, but does not explain that shifting budget from training to inference can improve performance at the same total cost when spending is heavily skewed toward training.
